canonicalExplanation.summary: A full page load tells everyone something changed: the tab title updates, screen readers announce the new page, and focus starts at the top. A client-side route change does **none of that by itself**; React just swaps components. So for each route, **set `document.title`** to describe the view, and after navigation **move focus to the main heading** (given `tabIndex={-1}` so it can be focused without joining the Tab order). Don't move focus on the very first load, and don't trap it: the next Tab should continue naturally from there.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A screen-reader user clicks "CSS Basics" in the course list. The content changes, but they hear nothing, focus stays on the link that's no longer on screen, and the tab still says "Courses". After a course route changes, the main heading receives managed focus without trapping subsequent navigation. In this lesson you'll verify route changes are perceivable to keyboard and assistive-technology users.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Remote data and asynchronous UI** module, **URL and history state**, **Declarative routes and links**, **Refs and imperative escape hatches**, and **Title and descriptive metadata**.

sections.heading: The model: title, then focus the heading
Check it

includes: Move focus to the main heading after client navigation without trapping it, and test it.

outcomes: Verify route changes are perceivable to keyboard and assistive-technology users.

examples.title: Arriving on the new course page
examples.situation: After a course route changes, the main heading receives managed focus without trapping subsequent navigation.
walkthrough: **Managed focus:** RouteHeading focuses the h1 with tabIndex -1 after each navigation, but not on the first page load.
**Check:** a test will click the course link and assert the h1 is focused; pressing Tab will then reach the first link in the page.
examples.result: Screen-reader users hear "CSS Basics, heading level 1", the tab title matches, and keyboard navigation continues normally.

examples.title: The title stuck on Home
examples.situation: Every page's browser tab says "Codestead | Home", so learners with several tabs can't tell them apart, and history entries all look the same.
walkthrough: The title was set once in index.html and never updated.
Each route should set its own title.
Call usePageTitle in each page component with its specific name.
examples.result: Tabs and history entries show the page each one is on.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Changing visible React components automatically announces a new page to assistive technology.
misconceptions.correction: Swapping components changes the DOM silently. Without a title update and a focus move (or an announcement), screen-reader and keyboard users don't learn that the view changed.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Arriving on the new course page", what did the screen-reader user hear?

analogy.example: Client navigation is like **changing the slides in a presentation without saying "next slide"**. People looking at the screen notice; people listening don't. Updating the title and focusing the heading is **saying the new slide's name out loud**.
usefulFor: heading focus = saying the slide title
limitations: Presenters don't trap the audience; focus must not trap Tab.
The first slide doesn't need an announcement: the page load did it.

steps.explanation: The learner activates a link in the course list.
The course route changes and the new view renders.
The main heading receives managed focus without trapping subsequent navigation.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing a perceivable route change. Step 1, Click: focus is course link; title is Courses | Codestead. The learner activates a link in the course list. Step 2, Render: view is CoursePage. The course route changes and the new view renders. Step 3, Effects: title is CSS Basics | Codestead; focus is h1 CSS Basics. The main heading receives managed focus without trapping subsequent navigation.

nearTransfer.prompt: Add usePageTitle and RouteHeading to a lesson page and a not-found page, so both set titles and focus their h1 after navigation.

farTransfer.prompt: Audit a routed app with a keyboard and screen reader: for three navigations, record title, what's announced and where focus lands. Fix the gaps and add tests for title and focus.
expectedEvidence: An audit table before and after.

remediation.explanation: After every route change ask: **Does the tab title name this view? Where is focus? Would a screen-reader user know the page changed?**
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The title stuck on Home".

recap.summary: To verify route changes are perceivable, set document.title for each view, move focus to the main heading (tabIndex -1) after client navigation but not on first load, keep Tab order flowing from there, and test the title and document.activeElement after clicking links.
